subject: Architecture
title: Sick Building Syndrome: When Architecture Hurts
description: A 60-second lesson on Sick Building Syndrome: When Architecture Hurts.

hook.text: Millions of workers feel headaches, fatigue, and nausea at the office — and feel fine as soon as they leave.

buildup.text: Sealed buildings trap volatile compounds from carpets, paint, furniture, and cleaning products.

discovery.text: The EPA found indoor air can be 2-5 times more polluted than outdoor air, even in major cities.

twist.text: Energy-efficient buildings sealed tighter to save power actually made indoor air quality worse.

climax.text: Green building standards now require low-VOC materials and fresh air ventilation rates to protect health.

punchline.text: We sealed buildings to save energy and poisoned the people inside.

quiz.question: How does indoor air quality compare to outdoor air?
options: Indoor air is always cleaner due to filtration
Indoor air can be 2-5 times more polluted than outdoor air
They are roughly equal in most buildings

details.summary: Sick Building Syndrome (SBS) describes symptoms — headaches, fatigue, respiratory irritation — experienced by occupants that improve after leaving the building.
details.whyItMatters: People spend roughly 90% of their time indoors, making indoor air quality a direct health issue. SBS reveals that energy-efficient buildings sealed tightly to reduce heat loss can inadvertently trap pollutants.
takeaways: Symptoms include headaches, fatigue, and respiratory irritation
Indoor air can be 2-5 times more polluted than outdoor air
Tight energy-efficient buildings can trap pollutants inside

faq.question: What causes Sick Building Syndrome?
faq.answer: Inadequate ventilation is the most common cause. Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) off-gassing from carpets, paints, furniture, and cleaning products accumulate in poorly ventilated spaces. Biological contaminants from HVAC systems, mold, and dust mites add to the problem.

faq.question: How can architects design healthier buildings?
faq.answer: Specify low-VOC materials and finishes. Design ventilation systems that provide adequate fresh air exchange. Use operable windows where possible. Maintain HVAC systems diligently. Include air filtration beyond minimum code requirements.
